intro: Section 29.1 covers death, dying and bereavement: how death is defined (the 1981 Uniform Determination of Death Act and brain death criteria), the legal duties after a death and the psychological autopsy, Kübler-Ross's stages of dying and near-death experiences, how children, adolescents and adults understand and face death, then normal grief and mourning, anticipatory grief and anniversary reactions, complicated grief and its types, grief versus major depression and PTSD, the biology and phases of grief, bereavement across the life cycle, and grief therapy. Update boxes add the 2023 US brain death guideline and prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR and ICD-11). Chapter 20 covers uncomplicated bereavement as a condition of clinical attention.
objectives: State the two legal routes to death under the 1981 standard and the bedside findings of brain death.
Describe the five Kübler-Ross stages and how a clinician should respond at each, without treating them as a fixed order.
Explain how preschool children, school-age children, adolescents and older adults understand death.
Define grief, mourning, bereavement, anticipatory grief and anniversary reactions, and describe the normal course of grief.
Tell normal grief from major depressive disorder, complicated grief types and PTSD after a violent death.
Recognize the medical risks after bereavement, the phases of grief, and how children grieve at each age.
Choose the right help for a bereaved person: support, a sleep aid, grief therapy, self-help groups or psychiatric referral.
